candidates.name: CONNECTION TO THE EARTH
candidates.description: Buildings that touch the ground directly feel grounded and connected; those raised on stilts or slabs feel alienated. Maps to software systems that maintain direct contact with their underlying data/infrastructure vs. those abstracted away from it.

candidates.name: GARDEN GROWING WILD
candidates.description: A garden that grows true to its own laws is neither wilderness nor entirely artificial. Maps to codebases and organizations that balance deliberate structure with organic evolution.

candidates.name: ALCOVES
candidates.description: Large undifferentiated rooms fail to support varied activities; internal subdivision into smaller defined zones (alcoves) is necessary. Maps to namespaces, modules, bounded contexts.

candidates.name: WINDOW PLACE
candidates.description: A window that becomes a place (bay window, window seat) draws people to the boundary between inside and outside. Maps to interfaces thick enough to inhabit -- dashboards, REPLs, preview panes.

candidates.name: WORKSPACE ENCLOSURE
candidates.description: People cannot work effectively if their workspace is too enclosed or too exposed. The balance between privacy and connection maps to developer environments, team structures, and information boundaries.

candidates.name: SITTING CIRCLE
candidates.description: Seating arranged in a rough circle with varied chairs and protected positioning gathers life around it; rows and sterile arrangements kill interaction. Maps to meeting formats, team topologies, and collaborative tool design.

candidates.name: CEILING HEIGHT VARIETY
candidates.description: Uniform ceiling height makes a building uncomfortable; varying heights signal different social functions (high for gatherings, low for intimacy). Maps to varying levels of abstraction and ceremony across different parts of a system.

candidates.name: WINDOWS OVERLOOKING LIFE
candidates.description: Rooms without a view are prisons. Windows must overlook human activity, not blank walls. Maps to observability, monitoring dashboards, and the need for systems to provide visibility into the living activity they serve.

candidates.name: THICK WALLS
candidates.description: Thin, smooth walls feel dead and impersonal; thick walls with niches, shelves, and seats become usable surfaces. Maps to rich interface boundaries in software -- APIs, module boundaries, and abstraction layers that carry useful affordances.

candidates.name: SECRET PLACE
candidates.description: People need concealed, private spaces -- hidden corners, attics, garden nooks. Maps to hidden features, easter eggs, internal tools, and the need for private experimental spaces in systems and organizations.

candidates.name: STRUCTURE FOLLOWS SOCIAL SPACES
candidates.description: Physical structure (columns, walls) must align with social spaces (activities, groups). Maps directly to Conway's Law: software architecture mirrors organizational communication structure.

candidates.name: GOOD MATERIALS
candidates.description: Industrial materials are cheap but degrade ungracefully; natural materials age well and can be repaired locally. Maps to technology choices -- languages, frameworks, libraries -- that age well vs. those that become unmaintainable.

candidates.name: GRADUAL STIFFENING
candidates.description: Buildings should start loose and fluid, then stiffen incrementally as design decisions are validated. Maps to iterative development, progressive hardening of APIs, and the shift from prototype to production.

candidates.name: NATURAL DOORS AND WINDOWS
candidates.description: Window and door positions should be determined by the life inside the room, not by an abstract elevation drawing. Maps to API surface design driven by actual usage patterns rather than theoretical symmetry.

candidates.name: DEEP REVEALS
candidates.description: Windows set in thick walls create deep reveals -- a transition zone that softens glare and frames the view. Maps to boundaries between software components that carry rich contextual information rather than being flat interfaces.

candidates.name: FILTERED LIGHT
candidates.description: Light filtered through leaves or lattice is more beautiful and comfortable than direct light. Maps to mediated access to complex systems -- abstractions, summaries, curated views that filter raw complexity.

candidates.name: SMALL PANES
candidates.description: Plate glass windows that were supposed to connect us to nature actually disconnect us by removing the sense of boundary. Small panes provide both view and shelter. Maps to chunked interfaces, pagination, and bounded views.

candidates.name: ORNAMENT
candidates.description: People instinctively decorate their surroundings; the modernist removal of ornament creates sterile environments. Maps to code comments, ASCII art, custom error messages, and expressive touches in technical systems.

candidates.name: DIFFERENT CHAIRS
candidates.description: Identical chairs serve no one well because people are different sizes and sit differently. Maps to one-size-fits-all tools, processes, and interfaces vs. providing varied options that accommodate different working styles.

candidates.name: POOLS OF LIGHT
candidates.description: Uniform illumination destroys the social nature of space; pools of light create islands of activity. Maps to focused attention in interfaces, spotlight features, and the principle that not everything should be equally visible.

candidates.name: THINGS FROM YOUR LIFE
candidates.description: Rooms should contain objects that matter personally to their occupants, not decorator-chosen decor. Maps to personalized workspaces, dotfiles, custom tooling, and the principle that tools should reflect their user's history.
